title: How Does an Airplane Stay Up in the Sky?
question: How does an airplane stay up in the sky?
answer: Engines push the plane forward fast. Its wings push the rushing air down, so the air pushes the wings up. This upward push is called lift, and it balances the pull of gravity.

visual.what: Huy, Hùng, Bối and Beo sit on a grassy hill near an airport, looking up as a huge white airliner flies overhead. Bối points up, and Beo holds a little toy car.

parts.text: Huy, look at that plane! It's enormous and super heavy. Why doesn't it just drop out of the sky like a rock?
Like my toy car when I drop it!
Great question, Bối. And here's a surprise. The secret helper holding it up is something you can't even see.

visual.what: Huy smiles at the camera. Behind him Hùng carries a big cardboard box full of things: a ball, paper, a balloon and a cardboard wing.

parts.text: Today we'll find out how an airplane stays up in the sky. We'll meet four pushes and pulls, find out what wings really do, and then you can try a little test at home.
And I've brought a whole box of things to show you!

visual.what: On the left, a party balloon floats up. On the right, a heavy airplane sits on a giant weighing scale. Bối holds a balloon string.

parts.text: I know! A plane is full of air, so it floats like a balloon.
Nice thinking! Some balloons really do float up. But a plane is much heavier than the air around it. People call it a heavier-than-air machine. So it can't float up like a balloon does.

visual.what: A side view of a jet plane with arrows showing air blowing backward out of the engines and a big arrow pushing the plane forward. In a small thought bubble above Beo, a smiling giant holds a plane on a string.

parts.text: Then the engines must push it straight up!
Or a giant holds it up with a long string!

Two great guesses! There's no giant, Beo. But engines are very important. Look which way they point. They blow backward, so they push the plane forward, not up. Something else does the lifting. Let's find out what.

visual.what: Huy stands beside a big drawing of a plane with four empty arrow outlines around it, pointing up, down, forward and back.

parts.text: A plane in the sky feels four pushes and pulls at the same time. Scientists call them forces. A force is just a push or a pull.

visual.what: Hùng lets go of a red ball and it drops to the floor. A downward arrow labelled gravity points toward the ground. Bối laughs, holding an empty ice cream cone.

parts.text: The first force is gravity. Gravity pulls everything down toward the ground. It's why your ball falls when you let go of it.
Watch. I let go, and down it goes!
And that's why my ice cream ends up on the floor.

visual.what: The plane drawing now has a big golden arrow pointing up from the wings, labelled lift, with a little star next to it.

parts.text: The second force pushes up. It's called lift. Lift is the force that keeps a plane in the air. It's the star of today's story.

visual.what: The plane drawing with a forward arrow labelled thrust coming from the engines and a backward arrow labelled drag, with little wind lines brushing the plane.

parts.text: The third force is thrust. Thrust pushes the plane forward. It comes from propellers or jet engines. The fourth force is drag. Drag pulls backward. It's mostly the air rubbing against the plane, like when you run into a strong wind.

visual.what: A tug of war drawn on a plane. A team labelled lift pulls up and a team labelled gravity pulls down. Three small pictures show the plane going up, going down, and flying level.

parts.text: So it's like a tug of war!
Exactly! If lift is stronger than gravity, the plane goes up. If gravity is stronger, the plane goes down. When they're equal, the plane flies along at the same height.

visual.what: Huy holds up a card showing an up arrow and a down arrow of the same size, with an equals sign between them.

parts.text: So here's our first takeaway. To stay up, a plane needs lift that's as strong as gravity.

visual.what: Side by side, water flowing past a stone in a stream, and wavy air lines flowing past a wing. Bối holds her small toy plane.

parts.text: But where does lift come from? My toy plane doesn't lift anything.
Lift is made when air flows past a wing. Air is a fluid. A fluid is anything that can flow, like water. Air flows too, we just can't see it.

visual.what: A magnifying circle zooms into empty-looking air and shows lots of tiny round dots bouncing around. Beo peers at it with wide eyes.

parts.text: Air looks like nothing at all. But zoom in and it's made of countless tiny bits, much too small to see. When something moves fast through the air, it bumps into loads of them.
Air has bits? I can't see any!

visual.what: A plane speeds down a long runway. Air lines rush faster and faster over the wings, then the nose lifts and the plane rises into the sky.

parts.text: That's why planes race down a long runway before they take off. The engines push the plane faster and faster, and more and more air rushes past the wings. Soon there's enough lift to beat gravity, and up it goes.

visual.what: A plane parked at an airport gate with no air lines around it. Bối and Hùng stand next to it, and Hùng gives the wheel a friendly pat.

parts.text: So a parked plane has no lift?
Almost none. With no air rushing past its wings, it just sits there. Speed comes first.

visual.what: Huy holds up a card with three pictures joined by arrows, an engine, then a speedometer, then wind lines over a wing.

parts.text: Second takeaway. Engines make speed, and speed makes air flow over the wings. No moving air, no lift.

visual.what: Hùng holds up a cardboard wing cut so we see it from the side. Labels point to the rounded front, the curved top, the thin back, and the slight upward tilt.

parts.text: Ta-da! I made a wing out of cardboard, so we can see it from the side.
Thanks, Hùng. A wing is rounded at the front, curved on top, and thin at the back. And it's tipped up just a little at the front.

visual.what: Side view of the tilted wing moving through air. Blue air lines flow over and under it and bend downward as they leave the back of the wing.

parts.text: As the wing slices through the air, its shape and its tilt bend the air downward. Look at the air leaving the back of the wing. It's heading down.

visual.what: Hùng sits on a skateboard on a flat floor and pushes gently against a wall with both hands. He rolls slowly backward, looking surprised, while Beo laughs.

parts.text: Here's a rule of nature. When you push on something, it pushes back on you. Push gently on a wall while you sit on a skateboard and you roll away from it.
Whoa! I pushed the wall, and the wall pushed me back!
Bye bye, Hùng!

visual.what: The wing with blue arrows pushing air down behind it, and one big golden arrow labelled lift pushing the wing up.

parts.text: Wings work the same way. The wing pushes air down, so the air pushes the wing up. That upward push is lift!

visual.what: One tiny air dot with a tiny up arrow, then many dots with many small arrows, all adding up to one giant golden lift arrow under a big plane.

parts.text: But air is so light! How can it hold up a whole plane?
One tiny bit of air is very light. But big fast wings push a huge amount of air down every single second. All those little pushes add up to one giant lift.

visual.what: Huy holds up a card showing a wing with a down arrow for the air and an up arrow for the wing.

parts.text: Third takeaway. Wings push air down, and the air pushes the wings up.

visual.what: Beo stands in the middle of the picture with lots of small soft arrows pressing gently on him from every side, labelled air pressure.

parts.text: There's another way to look at the very same lift. It's called air pressure. Pressure means how hard something presses. Air is gently pressing on you right now, from every side.
The air is pressing on me? I don't feel it!
It's very gentle, Beo, and it presses from every side, so you don't notice it.

visual.what: A timeline from the year 1738 to today, with a friendly drawing of Daniel Bernoulli writing in a book at the start. Next to it, fast air lines labelled low pressure and slow air lines labelled high pressure.

parts.text: Air flowing over the top of a wing moves faster. About three hundred years ago, a scientist called Daniel Bernoulli wrote about a rule. When air or water flows faster, its pressure gets lower.

visual.what: Side view of the wing. A few small arrows press down on top, labelled low pressure. Many big arrows press up from underneath, labelled high pressure. A golden lift arrow points up.

parts.text: So the air on top presses down only gently. The air underneath presses up harder. The wing gets pushed up, and that's lift again.

visual.what: Two pictures of the same wing side by side, one showing air pushed down behind it, one showing pressure arrows. Both lead to the same golden lift arrow, and Bối looks from one to the other.

parts.text: Wait, so which one is right? Pushing air down, or pressure?

Both! They are two ways of describing the same lift. There are many ways to explain lift, some simpler than others, and some popular explanations have even been shown to be wrong. That's how science works.

visual.what: Huy holds up a card showing one wing with low pressure on top and air pushed down behind, joined to one golden lift arrow.

parts.text: Fourth takeaway. Lower pressure above the wing and air pushed down below it are two sides of the same lift.

visual.what: A funny picture of a giant airliner squeezed onto a tiny house driveway, its wings poking over the fence, next to a flower bed. Beside it, a long airport runway stretches far away.

parts.text: Imagine if a big plane tried to take off from your driveway.
It would never get fast enough! Not enough air on the wings.
And it would squash Mum's flowers!
Exactly. That's why airports have such long runways. Planes need room to speed up.

visual.what: Hùng kneels at a table with two sheets of paper. He folds one into a paper plane and squashes the other into a ball, in a clear, empty room.

parts.text: Now a test you can try at home. Take two sheets of paper. Fold one into a paper plane and squash the other into a ball. Find a clear space, make sure nobody is in front of you, and throw them both gently.
One paper plane, one paper ball. Ready!

visual.what: Hùng's first paper plane loops round in a circle and lands softly on top of his own head. Bối and Beo giggle.

parts.text: Hey! My plane came back and landed on my head!
It likes you, Hùng!
Throw it straight and gently this time.

visual.what: Hùng throws again. The paper ball drops straight to the floor near him, while the paper plane glides in a long smooth line across the room. Little arrows show air pushed down under its wings.

parts.text: The ball dropped fast, but the plane glided all the way across the room!
The wings pushed air down, so the air held the plane up a little longer. A paper plane has no engine, so your throw is its thrust.

visual.what: Huy stands beside the plane drawing with all four arrows filled in, thrust, drag, lift and gravity, with the lift arrow glowing.

parts.text: So how does a plane stay up? Engines push it forward fast, its wings push the rushing air down, and the air pushes the wings up. That lift balances gravity.

visual.what: On the left, an airplane wing with a lift arrow pointing up. On the right, a race car with a wing on its back and a lift arrow pointing down, pressing it onto the road on a curve.

parts.text: Fun fact! Lift doesn't always point up. Race cars have wings too, but theirs make lift that pushes down. It holds the car tight against the road so it can zoom round corners.
An upside-down airplane wing on a car? So cool!
I want one on my bike!

visual.what: Huy, Hùng, Bối and Beo wave at the camera. A small helicopter hovers in a thought bubble, and a big button says Subscribe to Ask Huy.

parts.text: Next time, we'll find out how a helicopter can hover in one spot. Subscribe to Ask Huy so you don't miss it, and keep asking questions!
Bye! Go throw some paper planes!
Bye bye!

facts.claim: Lift is the upward force that keeps an aircraft in the air; it is made when a fluid like air flows past a solid object like a wing.
The simplest explanation of lift is that the wing pushes air downward and the reaction pushes the wing up.
There are several ways to explain lift, some more complicated than others, and some have been shown to be false.
Lift can point in any direction; the wing on a race car makes lift that points down.
Lift pushes up and gravity pulls down; if lift is stronger the plane goes up, if gravity is stronger the plane goes down.
In planes, lift is caused by airflow over the wings.
Thrust pushes forward and is usually made by propellers or jets; drag pushes backward and is mostly caused by air friction.
Airplanes are heavier-than-air machines pushed forward by thrust from a jet engine or propeller.
In a flowing fluid, faster speed goes together with lower pressure.
Daniel Bernoulli published the principle in his book Hydrodynamica in 1738, about three hundred years ago.
A force is a push or a pull; gravity pulls things down toward the ground; air is a fluid made of tiny particles that presses from all sides; when you push on something it pushes back.
Air flows faster over the top of a wing, and planes need speed on a runway to make enough lift to take off.

description: How can a huge, heavy airplane stay up in the sky? Join Huy, his helper Hùng, Bối and little Beo to meet the four forces of flight and find out how wings push air down so the air pushes them up. It ends with a safe paper plane test you can try at home, and it's a simple first look at how flight works for children aged 6–12.

cast.name: Huy
cast.role: the host (25): curious, warm, a little funny; explains

cast.name: Hùng
cast.role: Huy's younger brother (21), his hands-on assistant: sets up and runs the experiments and demos, brings things, now and then a funny little mishap

cast.name: Bối
cast.role: an 8-year-old girl who asks, guesses and tries things

cast.name: Beo
cast.role: Bối's 5-year-old little brother: curious, makes funny innocent guesses
